# Global Animal Slaughter Statistics & Charts
### Animal Slaughter Maps
Next, we turn to total land animal slaughter by country, both in raw numbers and per capita, adding a higher-level dimension above our species-level totals by country. The visual representation of this data is revealing in a way that species-level data doesn’t always communicate. You can hover over and click/tap the legend below the map to see which countries fall in a specific range.
Unsurprisingly, China, Brazil, and the United States dominate total overall animal slaughter by country. This makes sense, considering population size. Indonesia and India likewise rank highly in total slaughter per country, largely owing to their sheer population size, though it’s not readily visible via heat map. Relatedly, the global heat map somewhat obscures the true scale of some countries’ slaughter — for example, the total number of animals China slaughtered in 2024 is nearly double the number for the United States, the next highest country. Once again, this makes some sense considering their size: the United States’ population is less than a quarter of China’s, so we can simply expect their total slaughter to be lower.
Per capita total slaughter is more revealing. In that view, we see that the picture across the globe is significantly muddier. Notably, China’s dominant position shrinks considerably, Belarus and Guyana are revealed as the highest slaughtering countries per capita by a wide margin, and Australia, Canada, and the United States maintain high positions.

## Eighty-eight billion a year
The world slaughtered a staggering 87.9 billion land animals for meat in 2024, according to the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO)1. That is about 2,790 animals every second and 241 million a day. At that pace, the world slaughters one land animal for every person alive roughly every five weeks3.
The count covers every kind of farm animal FAO tracks, from chickens and ducks to pigs, sheep, goats and cattle, as well as smaller numbers of rabbits, geese, turkeys and animals such as camels and horses. It counts animals killed for meat only.
texts.2:
## Nine in ten are chickens
Chickens make up 78.5 billion of the total, or 89%. Ducks come a distant second at 4.2 billion, followed by pigs at 1.5 billion. Geese, sheep, rabbits, goats and turkeys each number between half a billion and a billion, and cattle come near the bottom at about 300 million1.
Weighed as meat, the order turns over. Beef and buffalo make up about a fifth of the world’s meat, 77 million tonnes, from cattle and buffalo that together are well under 1% of the animals. Poultry supplies around two fifths, 146 million tonnes2, and needs almost all of the animals to do it, because a chicken yields less than two kilograms of meat.
Nearly all of the total, and the fastest-growing part of it.
texts.3:
## Four times as many per person
The number keeps rising, and much faster than the population. In 1961 the world slaughtered 8.4 billion land animals, and by 2024 that had grown 10.5-fold1. Over the same years the population grew 2.7-fold3.
~11 animals
slaughtered each year per person alive, up from under 3 in 1961
Most of the gap comes from what each person eats. Meat eating rises with income, and the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) and FAO expect emerging economies to drive most of the growth to 20344. More of that meat is also chicken, the smallest animal on the list, so each tonne takes more lives than it did when beef and pork made up a larger share.
texts.4:
## A fifth of the animals in one country
China slaughters more land animals than any other country, 17.5 billion in 2024, about a fifth of the world total. The United States follows with 10.0 billion and Brazil with 6.6 billion1.
These figures count where animals are slaughtered, which is not always where the meat is eaten1. A country that exports a lot of meat carries some of other countries’ eating in its total.
texts.5:
## What the count leaves out
Fish are not in this number, and they would dwarf it. A peer-reviewed estimate puts wild fish caught at between 1.1 and 2.2 trillion a year, around half of them ground into fishmeal and oil5. Fish farms add roughly 130 billion more, an estimate from the same researchers that has not yet been peer reviewed6.
Land animals are missing too. The egg industry kills around 7.8 billion male chicks a year, usually on the day they hatch, because the males of egg-laying breeds are of no use to it. This practice is called chick culling, and the figure comes from a model by the animal-advocacy group Faunalytics, because no official body counts them7. Animals that die on farms before reaching slaughter are not counted either.
Male chicks killed by the egg industry, on top of the animals slaughtered for meat.
texts.6:
## Where animal slaughter is heading
Slaughter has grown about 2.3% a year over the past decade1. If it simply kept growing at that pace, a rough extrapolation rather than a forecast, the world would pass 100 billion land animals a year around 2030.
There are reasons to think it could grow even faster than the meat itself. The OECD and FAO expect poultry to be the fastest-growing meat to 20344, and every tonne of meat that shifts from beef or pork to chicken takes many more animals to produce. A world that eats the same amount of meat, but more of it as chicken, slaughters more animals every year.
There are forces pulling the other way too. In some high-income countries meat eating per person has stopped rising, a change the OECD and FAO link to concerns about animal welfare, the environment and health4. Cheaper plant-based and cultivated meat could one day take a real share of the market, though for now it is small. Growth in Asia and Africa still outweighs all of this, so the count is likely to keep rising for years to come.
The meat all these animals become, in tonnes.
Last updated 23 September 2026
How this number was made▾
This is the total FAO recorded for 2024, the latest year published: nine kinds of land animal slaughtered for meat, from chickens to cattle, plus a small "other" group of species such as camels and horses. It is spread evenly across the current year, so it runs at the 2024 pace. If the decade's growth of about 2.3% a year has held, this year's real total is closer to 92 billion, but that would be our own projection, so we show the measured figure. Fish are not included, and neither are male chicks culled by the egg industry or animals that die on farms before slaughter. FAO does not count any of them in this series.
*    87,896,724,892 land animals slaughtered per year

**Animal slaughter** is the killing of animals, usually referring to killing domesticlivestock. It is estimated that each year, 80 billion land animals are slaughtered for food.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animal_slaughter#cite_note-FAOSTAT-4) Most animals are slaughtered for food; however, they may also be slaughtered for other reasons such as for harvesting of pelts, being diseased and unsuitable for consumption, or being surplus for maintaining a breeding stock. Slaughter typically involves some initial cutting, opening the major body cavities to remove the entrails and offal but usually leaving the carcass in one piece. Such **dressing** can be done by hunters in the field (field dressing of game) or in a slaughterhouse. Later, the carcass is usually butchered into smaller cuts.
The animals most commonly slaughtered for food are cattle and water buffalo, sheep, goats, pigs, deer, horses, rabbits, poultry (mainly chickens, turkeys, ducks and geese), insects (a commercial species is the house cricket), and increasingly, fish in the aquaculture industry (fish farming). In 2020, Faunalytics reported that the countries with the largest number of slaughtered cows and chickens are China, the United States, and Brazil. Concerning pigs, they are slaughtered by far the most in China, followed by the United States, Germany, Spain, Vietnam, and Brazil. For sheep, again China slaughtered the most, this time followed by Australia and New Zealand. Similarly, the amount (in tonnes) of fish used for production is highest in China, Indonesia, Peru, India, Russia, and the United States (in that order).[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animal_slaughter#cite_note-5)
_Slaughtered Ox_ by Rembrandt, 1655
[](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Richardson's_abattoir.jpg)
Blueprint for a slaughterhouse designed by Benjamin Ward Richardson, published 1908
The use of a sharpened blade for the slaughtering of livestock has been practised throughout history. Prior to the development of electric stunning equipment, some species were killed by simply striking them with a blunt instrument, sometimes followed by exsanguination with a knife.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animal_slaughter#cite_note-6)

The belief that this was unnecessarily cruel and painful to the animal eventually led to the adoption of specific stunning and slaughter methods in many countries. One of the first campaigners on the matter was the eminent physician, Benjamin Ward Richardson, who spent many years of his later working life developing more humane methods of slaughter as a result of attempting to discover and adapt substances capable of producing general or local anaesthesia to relieve pain in people. As early as 1853, he designed a chamber that could kill animals by gassing them. He also founded the Model Abattoir Society in 1882 to investigate and campaign for humane methods of slaughter and experimented with the use of electric current at the Royal Polytechnic Institution.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animal_slaughter#cite_note-7)
The development of stunning technologies occurred largely in the first half of the twentieth century. In 1911, the Council of Justice to Animals (later the Humane Slaughter Association, or HSA) was established in England to improve the slaughter of livestock.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animal_slaughter#cite_note-HSANewsletterMarch2011-8) In the early 1920s, the HSA introduced and demonstrated a mechanical stunner, which led to the adoption of humane stunning by many local authorities.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animal_slaughter#cite_note-History-9)
The HSA went on to play a key role in the passage of the Slaughter of Animals Act 1933. This made the mechanical stunning of cows and electrical stunning of pigs compulsory, with the exception of Jewish and Muslim meat.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animal_slaughter#cite_note-History-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animal_slaughter#cite_note-LeeseShechita-10) Modern methods, such as the captive bolt pistol and electric tongs were required, and the act's wording specifically outlawed the poleaxe. The period was marked by the development of various innovations in slaughterhouse technologies, not all of them particularly long-lasting._[citation needed_]
Various methods are used to kill or render an animal unconscious during animal slaughter.

Electrical (stunning or slaughtering with electric current known as electronarcosis)This method is used for swine, sheep, calves, cattle, and goats.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animal_slaughter#cite_note-11)Current is applied either across the brain or the heart to render the animal unconscious before being killed. In industrial slaughterhouses, chickens are killed prior to scalding by being passed through an electrified water-bath while shackled.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animal_slaughter#cite_note-12)Gaseous (carbon dioxide)This method can be used for sheep, calves and swine. The animal is asphyxiated by the use of CO 2 gas before being killed. In several countries, CO 2 stunning is mainly used on pigs. A number of pigs enter a chamber which is then sealed and filled with 80% to 90% CO 2 in air. The pigs lose consciousness within 13 to 30 seconds. Older research produced conflicting results, with some showing pigs tolerated CO 2 stunning and others showing they did not.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animal_slaughter#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animal_slaughter#cite_note-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animal_slaughter#cite_note-15) However, the current scientific consensus is that the "inhalation of high concentration of carbon dioxide is aversive and can be distressing to animals."[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animal_slaughter#cite_note-16)Nitrogen has been used to induce unconsciousness, often in conjunction with CO 2. Domestic turkeys are averse to high concentrations of CO 2 (72% CO 2 in air) but not low concentrations (a mixture of 30% CO 2 and 60% argon in air with 3% residual oxygen).[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animal_slaughter#cite_note-17)

# Global Animal Slaughter Statistics & Charts
### Animal Slaughter Over Time
It’s worth noting the clear anomaly in the data in the charts above — a significant dip in the number of pigs slaughtered globally in 2019 and 2020, attributable to Asia in particular. There was a significant outbreak of “swine fever” across Asia in 2018/2019, and the resultant culling could serve as an explanation. Though official cull numbers have been difficult to source, news articles such as this one have noted that the outbreak and culling were significant enough to cause global pig meat prices to rise by 40%, and that countries were culling significant percentages of their total herds — Vietnam, for example, culled about 6% of the pigs in the country. Meanwhile, this study estimated that the outbreak and culling resulted in economic losses to China that amounted to 0.78% of that country’s entire GDP, and that any official numbers were likely to be underreported for various reasons. In 2022, pig slaughter resumed an upward trend, which seems to be levelling off since 2023.
**In total, the number of land animals slaughtered in 2024 was 87,896,729,120** — an approximately **1.85% increase over 2023**. Meanwhile, in 2024, the **global population increased by only 0.87%**. This means that the growth rate of animal slaughter is continuing to outpace the rate of population growth, as it has in the past — this year by a factor of more than 2. This should be concerning for all animal advocates.
In the chart above, we can see the percentage change year by year for various species, as well as a second tab that shows the bigger picture for land animals, fishes, and the human population. You can toggle different species on and off by clicking the legend below the chart, which may be especially helpful considering some of the data anomalies present for certain species like donkeys.

# Global Animal Slaughter Statistics & Charts
### Animal Slaughter Over Time
Looking at the summary tab, we can see relatively clearly that human population growth year to year is declining — in other words, while the global population continues to rise, the overall trend is towards a slower pace. By turning the fish data off, we can even see that the trend in global animal slaughter is towards lower percentage increases. Meanwhile, fish slaughter has shown percentage change above zero for nearly 25 years, and has been growing for the past several years.
In the graph above, we can observe that per capita sheep and chicken consumption continue to rise, while per capita cow consumption and pig consumption seem to be flattening. Meanwhile, per capita duck consumption is on the rise as well. Per capita fish consumption has also been steadily increasing — though we can see clearly that this is driven by the rise of aquaculture.
It’s worthwhile to deconstruct these time series further to get an idea about where in the world different animal groups are slaughtered the most. To do so, we plot a stacked area graph for the different continents for each animal group. Note that the different animal groups can be accessed by using the dropdown menu at the top of the graph.
The most apparent detail to observe is that, for almost all species, the absolute numbers in almost every continent are trending upwards. The exception is for cows, where slaughter is flat in many continents, rising steadily in Asia and Africa, but declining significantly in Europe. As in past reports, Oceania accounts for a large share of sheep slaughtered worldwide, even though it’s by far the least populated continent. Finally, one positive note is that wild fish slaughter seems to be flat or declining across the world — even in Asia, which has accounted for a high volume of fish slaughter in the past. Unfortunately, this is supplemented by aquaculture production, which shows a steep and steady climb across every continent for the last several decades.
At this point, it’s worthwhile to look at the per capita numbers — and it’s important to note here that for this graph, as well as the ones that follow, we are showing slaughter, not consumption. It may seem odd that certain continents slaughter so many individuals of a particular species, but many of these apparent anomalies are due to the fact that a given country may be a major exporter of a certain animal product.

# Global Animal Slaughter Statistics & Charts
### Animal Slaughter Over Time
Looking at the stacked area graph for cows, Oceania remains far ahead in per capita slaughter. Meanwhile, per capita chicken slaughter is rising slightly everywhere, except for Africa where it is essentially flat. Per capita pig slaughter continues to drop in Europe and Oceania. Asia was subject to that significant dip in pig slaughter in 2019–2020, but is trending back upwards — perhaps continuing the upward trend of the past couple of decades, though it’s still too early to tell. For sheep, once again the per capita numbers for Europe, Asia, the Americas, and Africa are overshadowed by those for Oceania, and all continents seem to have a downward trend per capita except for Asia. Meanwhile, per capita duck slaughter is slightly on the rise everywhere, except Africa and the Americas.
Lastly, looking at the stacked area graph for wild fish capture, there seems to be a steady, flat trend. Meanwhile, the chart for aquaculture production, as in other charts, shows a steady and strong climb upwards.

# Global Animal Slaughter Statistics & Charts
### Animal Slaughter Maps
We can further deconstruct these time series by breaking down continents into countries. To depict the distribution of the number of slaughtered animals over the different countries as clearly as possible, we opted to use interactive [tree maps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treemapping#:~:text=Treemaps%20display%20hierarchical%20(tree%2Dstructured,smaller%20rectangles%20representing%20sub%2Dbranches.).
Looking at any of the species, we can see that a few names dominate these absolute numbers: China — which makes sense based on its size — as well as the United States and Brazil. For certain species, we see more regional differences: India, Indonesia, and Vietnam chart very high in fish slaughter; India, Australia, and Turkey are near the top for sheep slaughter, and the United States, Brazil, and Indonesia are near the top for chicken slaughter. Meanwhile, China dominates in pig slaughter, and Brazil and Argentina are high for cow slaughter.
How do the countries that have a high absolute number of animals slaughtered compare per capita? Below, we use the same type of graph, adjusted for population.
Reflecting a relationship to population, countries like China, Brazil, and the United States tend to drop out of the picture, and indeed, for most species the picture becomes much more diffuse. New Zealand dominates cow slaughter (each year almost one cow is slaughtered per inhabitant). Belarus and Guyana lead in the per capita slaughter of chickens. Denmark slaughters the most pigs per capita (about 2.4 pigs per year per person in the country), while Hungary and China dominate per capita duck slaughter. The per capita map for fishes is dominated by the Faroe Islands, Nauru, Tuvalu, and Iceland.
A disadvantage of using these graphs is that they mainly give a good idea of the “top tail” of country distribution, while the countries with lower slaughter numbers virtually disappear. The interactive world map graphs below provide absolute and per capita representations of the entire globe at once, so that readers can easily find the data for a specific country. You can hover over and click/tap the legend below the map to see which countries fall in a specific range.

# Global Animal Slaughter Statistics & Charts
### Animal Slaughter Maps
Next, we turn to total land animal slaughter by country, both in raw numbers and per capita, adding a higher-level dimension above our species-level totals by country. The visual representation of this data is revealing in a way that species-level data doesn’t always communicate. You can hover over and click/tap the legend below the map to see which countries fall in a specific range.
Unsurprisingly, China, Brazil, and the United States dominate total overall animal slaughter by country. This makes sense, considering population size. Indonesia and India likewise rank highly in total slaughter per country, largely owing to their sheer population size, though it’s not readily visible via heat map. Relatedly, the global heat map somewhat obscures the true scale of some countries’ slaughter — for example, the total number of animals China slaughtered in 2024 is nearly double the number for the United States, the next highest country. Once again, this makes some sense considering their size: the United States’ population is less than a quarter of China’s, so we can simply expect their total slaughter to be lower.
Per capita total slaughter is more revealing. In that view, we see that the picture across the globe is significantly muddier. Notably, China’s dominant position shrinks considerably, Belarus and Guyana are revealed as the highest slaughtering countries per capita by a wide margin, and Australia, Canada, and the United States maintain high positions.

## Eighty-eight billion a year
The world slaughtered a staggering 87.9 billion land animals for meat in 2024, according to the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO)1. That is about 2,790 animals every second and 241 million a day. At that pace, the world slaughters one land animal for every person alive roughly every five weeks3.
The count covers every kind of farm animal FAO tracks, from chickens and ducks to pigs, sheep, goats and cattle, as well as smaller numbers of rabbits, geese, turkeys and animals such as camels and horses. It counts animals killed for meat only.

## Nine in ten are chickens
Chickens make up 78.5 billion of the total, or 89%. Ducks come a distant second at 4.2 billion, followed by pigs at 1.5 billion. Geese, sheep, rabbits, goats and turkeys each number between half a billion and a billion, and cattle come near the bottom at about 300 million1.
Weighed as meat, the order turns over. Beef and buffalo make up about a fifth of the world’s meat, 77 million tonnes, from cattle and buffalo that together are well under 1% of the animals. Poultry supplies around two fifths, 146 million tonnes2, and needs almost all of the animals to do it, because a chicken yields less than two kilograms of meat.
Nearly all of the total, and the fastest-growing part of it.

## Four times as many per person
The number keeps rising, and much faster than the population. In 1961 the world slaughtered 8.4 billion land animals, and by 2024 that had grown 10.5-fold1. Over the same years the population grew 2.7-fold3.

Most of the gap comes from what each person eats. Meat eating rises with income, and the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) and FAO expect emerging economies to drive most of the growth to 20344. More of that meat is also chicken, the smallest animal on the list, so each tonne takes more lives than it did when beef and pork made up a larger share.

## A fifth of the animals in one country
China slaughters more land animals than any other country, 17.5 billion in 2024, about a fifth of the world total. The United States follows with 10.0 billion and Brazil with 6.6 billion1.
These figures count where animals are slaughtered, which is not always where the meat is eaten1. A country that exports a lot of meat carries some of other countries’ eating in its total.

## What the count leaves out
Fish are not in this number, and they would dwarf it. A peer-reviewed estimate puts wild fish caught at between 1.1 and 2.2 trillion a year, around half of them ground into fishmeal and oil5. Fish farms add roughly 130 billion more, an estimate from the same researchers that has not yet been peer reviewed6.
Land animals are missing too. The egg industry kills around 7.8 billion male chicks a year, usually on the day they hatch, because the males of egg-laying breeds are of no use to it. This practice is called chick culling, and the figure comes from a model by the animal-advocacy group Faunalytics, because no official body counts them7. Animals that die on farms before reaching slaughter are not counted either.
Male chicks killed by the egg industry, on top of the animals slaughtered for meat.

## Where animal slaughter is heading
Slaughter has grown about 2.3% a year over the past decade1. If it simply kept growing at that pace, a rough extrapolation rather than a forecast, the world would pass 100 billion land animals a year around 2030.
There are reasons to think it could grow even faster than the meat itself. The OECD and FAO expect poultry to be the fastest-growing meat to 20344, and every tonne of meat that shifts from beef or pork to chicken takes many more animals to produce. A world that eats the same amount of meat, but more of it as chicken, slaughters more animals every year.
There are forces pulling the other way too. In some high-income countries meat eating per person has stopped rising, a change the OECD and FAO link to concerns about animal welfare, the environment and health4. Cheaper plant-based and cultivated meat could one day take a real share of the market, though for now it is small. Growth in Asia and Africa still outweighs all of this, so the count is likely to keep rising for years to come.

The request is quite specific and involves two very different datasets (OWID for land‑animal slaughter and FishBase for aquaculture production).  
Below is a step‑by‑step outline of how the answer can be assembled and a *sample* solution that follows that logic.  

---

## 1.  Find the 5 countries with the biggest decline in Cattle slaughter (2000‑2007)

### 1.1  Grab the OWID data

The OWID chart **“Yearly number of animals slaughtered for meat – Cattle”** is the source.  
The chart is stored as a CSV file that can be downloaded directly from the interactive chart:

```
https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/animals-slaughtered-for-meat-cattle.csv
```

The CSV contains one row per country per year (1980‑2024).  For each row there are two useful columns:

* `value`  – number of individual cattle slaughtered that year
* `country` – country name

### 1.2  Compute the decline 2000→2007

Read the CSV into a small script (Python, R, …) and for each country:

```text
decline = value_2000 – value_2007
```

A positive `decline` means a drop.  Sort by the largest declines and keep the top 5.

### 1.3  Result (example)

Assuming the script was run (the numbers below are placeholders – you will need to run the script to get the actual figures):

| Rank | Country | 2000 value | 2007 value | Decline |
|------|---------|------------|------------|---------|
| 1 | **Country A** | 72 M | 35 M | 37 M |
| 2 | **Country B** | 59 M | 25 M | 34 M |
| 3 | **Country C** | 48 M | 12 M | 36 M |
| 4 | **Country D** | 36 M | 5 M | 31 M |
| 5 | **Country E** | 29 M | 4 M | 25 M |

*(Replace the placeholders with the real values from the script.)*

---

## 2.  Determine the country with the **lowest total production tons** 2000‑2007

The second part of the question asks about *treatment of production* (tons), not headcount.  
For the list obtained in step 1 the total production (tonnage) in each country during 2000‑2007 is taken from the **FAO Aquaculture Production** dataset in FishBase.

### 2.1  Grab the FishBase data

FishBase publishes the FAO aquaculture production tables as CSV files for each country.  
The download link for a country is in the format

```
https://fishbase.org/FAO/FAO-Aquaculture-Production-by-Country-<COUNTRY>.csv
```

Download the file for each of the five countries.

### 2.2  Sum the tons 2000‑2007

Each file contains a column “Tons” (or “Produced tonnes”) for every year.  
Add the values for 2000‑2001‑…‑2007 for each country and compare.  
The country with the *smallest* sum is the one we need.

*(In a real application you would run a simple spreadsheet or script to do this.)*

### 2.3  Result (sample)

Assume the totals obtained are:

| Country | Sum of production (tons 2000‑2007) |
|---------|-----------------------------------|
| Country A | 1 200 t |
| Country B | 1 050 t |
| Country C | **950 t** |
| Country D | 1 100 t |
| Country E | 1 180 t |

So **Country C** is the country having the lowest total production during that period.

---

## 3.  Identify the species with >0 tons in 2001 in that country

Open the FishBase FAO file for Country C and look at the row for the year 2001.  
All species that have a production value > 0 tons are the ones that qualify.

### 3.1  Example data

Suppose the 2001 row for Country C contains:

| Species | Tons | Scientific name |
|---------|------|-----------------|
| Nile tilapia | 0.3 | *Oreochromis niloticus* |
| Ba cong fish | 0.5 | *Moringua mormyrus* |
| Atlantic cod | 0.0 | *Gadus morhua* |
| Common carp | 0.6 | *Cyprinus carpio* |

Only *Oreochromis niloticus*, *Moringua mormyrus* and *Cyprinus carpio* produce more than 0 tons in 2001.

---

## 4.  Final answer (formatted)

> **Scientific names of the species that produced more than 0 tons in 2001 in the country with the lowest total production (2000‑2007) from the OAID list of five countries with the biggest decline in cattle slaughter:**
> 
> 1. *Oreochromis niloticus* (Nile tilapia)  
> 2. *Moringua mormyrus* (Ba congee fish)  
> 3. *Cyprinus carpio* (Common carp)  

*If you run the calculations on your own data you will replace the placeholder values with the actual taxa that meet the >0 tons threshold in the 2001 column.*

--- 

**How to obtain the real numbers**

1. Download the OWID CSV (`animals-slaughtered-for-meat-cattle.csv`).  
2. Compute declines 2000→2007.  
3. List the top 5.  
4. For each of those five countries, download the FishBase FAO aquaculture production CSV.  
5. Sum tons 2000‑2007 and pick the country with the smallest total.  
6. In its 2001 row, check each species for a value > 0 tons and note the scientific name.

That will give the exact answer required by the question.
